A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RapVerse research, and their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. V1 includes Appendix A.1–A.6; v2 ends after its references without an appendix. This is an omission from the supplied document, not an extraction gap.

before.justification: V1 reports original motion and vocal generation results, main ablations, and tokenizer reconstruction experiments in Tables 2–5.

after.justification: V2 reports original generation and ablation results in Tables 2–3 and a motion user study in Figure 4.

M1.justification: Both retain three motion VQ-VAEs, the semantic/pitch/singer vocal tokenizer, and T5-conditioned autoregressive generation with the same token organization and decoding procedure. Omitting implementation descriptions from v1's appendix does not establish that those components were changed.

E1.justification: Both use the same English rap coverage: 108.44 hours of vocals from 32 singers and 26.8 hours of paired motion data. V2's user study samples existing RapVerse test clips, adding no dataset, domain or generation task.

E2.justification: Table 2(a) adds evaluated EMAGE and MotionCraft baselines while retaining the previous motion comparators and cascaded system. EMAGE was already discussed in v1 but had no reported comparison row. The vocal comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: The reported evaluation design gains a human ranking study with 20 participants, ten 10-second test videos, shuffled presentations, real-data references and four criteria. It loses the appendix's tokenizer reconstruction evaluations using MPJPE/PAMPJPE/ACCL and CER/GPE/VDE. The main 85%/7.5%/7.5% split and generation metrics remain unchanged; omitted training settings do not establish changed training procedures.

E4.justification: V1's Appendix A.4 and Tables 4–5 test motion and vocal codebook sizes, separate versus combined motion tokenizers through reconstruction, and singer-conditioned F0 preprocessing versus normalization. These analyses disappear from v2, although the generation-level ablations in Table 3 remain. Appendix A.5's additional qualitative examples are also omitted.

E5.justification: Both report identical vocal MOS values with 95% confidence intervals. Neither supplies repeated-run counts or seed information for the motion results. V2's user-study chart reports ranking percentages without introducing confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 2(a) revises RapVerse FID/DIV/BC from 18.65/12.19/0.481 to 17.58/14.08/0.485 and T2M-GPT FID from 18.42 to 23.45; RapVerse becomes highest-ranked on FID and DIV. Table 3 also changes values, including GT DIV from 12.53 to 14.53. V2 adds EMAGE/MotionCraft scores and user rankings favoring RapVerse on three criteria and TalkSHOW on expression synchronization. V1's Tables 4–5 results disappear, while vocal MOS remains identical. The reasons for the revised existing motion scores are unspecified.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, quantization rule and training objectives in Equations 1–5 retain their substance. Equation 3 replaces z with z^M to match the already introduced motion representation, a notation correction. No substantive theorem, proof or formal assumption is added or removed.

C1.justification: The introduction changes the dataset contribution from 'We release RapVerse' to 'We collect RapVerse,' dropping an explicit release claim. The central claims about joint generation from lyrics, modality tokenization and competitiveness with specialized systems remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 removes the explicit rap-only limitation, conditional applicability to other scenarios and multi-performer future direction from Section 6. It also drops the appendix's explanations of high character error rates, codebook and F0-conditioning tradeoffs, and specific misuse concerns. The main interpretations concerning cascaded errors and detailed facial representations remain.

D1.justification: V2 omits Appendix A.2–A.3, losing codebook sizes, loss weights, HuBERT layer selection, singer-conditioned F0 implementation, T5/decoder configurations, optimizer settings, training budgets and metric computation details. This substantially reduces reproducibility information. The project-page destination also changes; neither PDF establishes the current availability of external code or data.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations to Listen, Denoise, Action!, MotionCraft and DiffSHEG, with a brief MotionCraft discussion. Several appendix-related references, including LibriSpeech, librosa and VQ-VAE-2, disappear. These are limited updates; the broader positioning around unified text-conditioned vocal and motion generation remains stable.

P1.justification: The retained main prose and section order are largely unchanged. Local edits correct the title, update authors and affiliations, revise related-work wording and insert the user-study description. The limitations block and appendix are omitted, without extensive rewriting of the retained narrative.

P2.justification: V2 changes the document from single-column to two-column layout, moves Figure 1 above the abstract, and resizes or repositions retained displays. It adds the user-study chart as Figure 4 and omits v1's qualitative Figure 4 and Tables 4–5. Table 2 gains baseline rows, and Table 3's FGD heading becomes FID, consistent with the stated metric.

improvement.justification: The additional EMAGE/MotionCraft comparisons and human rankings strengthen motion evaluation. However, v2 loses the implementation details needed to reproduce the system, both tokenizer reconstruction studies, and explicit limitations, while leaving its revised motion scores unexplained. These losses in transparency and supporting evidence outweigh the bounded evaluation gains, although the core method and main experimental account remain intact.
